what-a-mortgage-is.audio-what-a-mortgage-is-g0-p0: Every loan officer works from a catalog — a whole shelf of mortgage products, each one a different way to get a client into a home. And no single product is right for everybody. Somebody's income, the house they've got their eye on, the down payment they've managed to save — any one of those can knock a product right off the list. So before you can pull the right one off the shelf for a borrower, you have to actually understand how a mortgage works underneath. That's where we start.
what-a-mortgage-is.audio-what-a-mortgage-is-g1-p0: Hardly anyone walks in and buys a house outright — the price tag is way more than most people are ever holding in the bank. So a lender puts up the money, and the buyer pays it back slowly, over a long stretch of years, often thirty. Now, what makes a lender comfortable handing three or four hundred thousand dollars to someone they barely know? The house itself. The house is what secures the loan. If the payments stop coming, the lender can take the property, sell it, and get its money back. That legal claim on the house — that's the lien. And the lien is the whole reason a lender will lend that much, for that long, at the rates they do.
what-a-mortgage-is.audio-what-a-mortgage-is-g2-p0: Every monthly payment is quietly doing two jobs at once. Part of it chips away at the principal — that's the actual amount you borrowed — and part of it is interest, the lender's charge for letting you use their money. Early on, a payment is almost all interest and the balance barely budges. Then over the years the mix tips the other way: more of each payment goes to principal, and the balance really starts to fall. Stretch that same loan over more years and each payment gets smaller, but you hand over more interest by the time it's done. Squeeze it into fewer years and the payments sting more each month, but the total interest comes out a good bit lower.
what-a-mortgage-is.audio-what-a-mortgage-is-g3-p0: The products themselves are all over the map. Some want twenty percent down; others ask for nothing at all. Some are backed by a bank, some by the government. Some hold one rate steady for the entire life of the loan, and others adjust it as the years roll by. A few you can draw on — the borrower pulls the money out in pieces, as it's needed, instead of all in one lump, kind of the way a credit card works. And with one of them it runs in reverse: instead of the homeowner paying the lender, the lender pays the homeowner. Every one of these was built for a particular kind of situation.
what-a-mortgage-is.audio-what-a-mortgage-is-g3-p1: Picture the people behind those loans. A veteran. A family buying out in a rural county. A first-timer who's scraped together three percent. A retiree sitting on decades of built-up equity. Someone financing a house that hasn't even been built yet. Each of those borrowers slots into a different loan — and matching the borrower to the right product, that's the job.

arms.audio-arms-g0-p0: An adjustable-rate mortgage — an A-R-M — starts you off with a low fixed rate for the first few years, and then it adjusts on a set schedule for the rest of the term. Lenders write it as two numbers. Something like five-one: the five is how many years the rate stays locked, and the one is how often it adjusts after that — here, once a year. Where the rate actually goes once it starts moving comes down to three things spelled out on the note: the index, the margin, and the caps.
arms.audio-arms-g1-p0: There are three caps on an A-R-M, and each one governs a different move. The initial cap limits that very first adjustment — how far the rate can jump the first time it changes. The periodic cap limits every adjustment after that one. And the life cap sets the ceiling, the highest the rate is ever allowed to climb, no matter what. One wrinkle: F-H-A and V-A ARMs don't carry an initial cap at all. On those loans, the periodic cap pulls double duty and governs that first adjustment too.

va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g0-p0: Of the four loan programs you'll work with, two lean on the federal government in a way the others don't — the government actually guarantees them, rather than insuring them or leaving them to the private market. On a V-A loan, the Department of Veterans Affairs stands behind it; on a U-S-D-A loan, the Department of Agriculture does. And that guaranty is what buys these two programs something even a conventional or an F-H-A loan can't offer — a borrower can put nothing down and still carry no mortgage insurance.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g1-p0: The V-A loan traces back to nineteen forty-four, when Congress passed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act to smooth the way home for World War Two veterans — and tucked inside it was the birth of V-A mortgage financing. A V-A residential mortgage loan is guaranteed through the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, and it plays by that agency's rules. But notice what the V-A doesn't do: it doesn't hand over the money, and it doesn't insure the loan. It simply promises the lender that if the veteran defaults, a slice of that loan is backed by the government.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g2-p0: A V-A loan isn't open to just anyone. The borrower has to be active military in good standing, or discharged as anything other than dishonorably, and they have to hold a Certificate of Eligibility — the C-O-E. That certificate reflects a basic entitlement of thirty-six thousand dollars, which means the V-A will guarantee a loan up to four times that entitlement. But four times isn't the borrowing ceiling. As long as the borrower qualifies, has full entitlement, and has no other active V-A loan running, there's no maximum loan limit at all — right up to the property's V-A Reasonable Value.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g3-p0: Conventional loans make you carry private mortgage insurance once the loan-to-value climbs past eighty percent, and F-H-A loans come with insurance baked in. V-A loans go the other way and ban mortgage insurance outright. In its place, the borrower pays a one-time V-A funding fee at settlement, and the V-A pools all those fees to pay lenders back when a borrower defaults — and if closing cash is tight, that fee can be folded right into the loan instead. Three things set the amount: whether it's a purchase or a refinance, how much the borrower puts down, and whether this is their first V-A loan or a repeat. For a first-use purchase with less than five percent down, the funding fee runs two point one five percent of the loan amount — so on a three hundred thousand dollar loan that's roughly sixty-four hundred fifty dollars — and it shrinks as the down payment grows. One more thing: escrow for taxes and insurance is mandatory on a V-A loan.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g4-p0: Some veterans skip that funding fee entirely — the ones the program most wants to shield. A veteran with a service-connected disability rated by the V-A at ten percent or more is exempt, and so is their immediate family. Same goes for an active member awarded the Purple Heart, and for certain surviving spouses of members killed or missing in action. Everyone else pays. And V-A loans never allow a prepayment penalty — the borrower can't be charged one, and the loan's proceeds can never be used to pay off a prepayment penalty on some other loan being refinanced away.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g5-p0: The V-A underwrites unlike anyone else, and it starts by ignoring the front-end housing ratio completely. It looks only at the back-end D-T-I, generally capped around forty-one percent, and that cap can stretch higher when residual income is strong. Residual income is simply what's left in the household's pocket each month after every mandatory expense is paid, and the V-A sets a minimum that shifts with the loan amount, the family size, and the region of the country. The thinking is down to earth — check whether a family actually has money left to live on, not just whether some ratio squeaks under a line.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g6-p0: V-A loans are fully assumable, and even a non-veteran can step in and take over a veteran's V-A mortgage. But there's a wrinkle worth knowing: since that assuming non-veteran has no C-O-E of their own, the original veteran's C-O-E stays locked to the loan until it's paid off in full — which means that veteran can't go get another V-A loan while it hangs there. The original veteran does walk away clean on the debt, though; they're no longer liable, and they keep no ownership in the property. And when it's time to refinance, the V-A offers the I-R-R-R-L — the Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan, or V-A Streamline — a light-documentation refinance built to knock the rate down.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g7-p0: Section five oh two of the U-S-D-A code is what sets up U-S-D-A home financing, and its whole reason for being is to push homeownership out into rural America. Just like the V-A loan, it's guaranteed by its agency — here the U.S. Department of Agriculture — not insured. A property only qualifies if it sits inside an approved U-S-D-A rural locale, and the U-S-D-A actually publishes an eligibility map you can check an address against. Like F-H-A, these loans welcome both traditional and non-traditional credit, and they finance primary residences only — no vacation homes, no rentals.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g8-p0: Congress only funds the U-S-D-A program with a set pot of money each year, so an income cap keeps it pointed at people of modest means: a household's income can't top one hundred fifteen percent of the adjusted area median income — the A-M-I — for that area. And because the whole thing is income-tested, a U-S-D-A applicant can't just decline to share what they earn. Any alimony, child support, or separate maintenance the borrower is legally entitled to has to go right on the application.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g9-p0: U-S-D-A loans ask for zero down — a full hundred percent loan-to-value — and, like V-A loans, they ban mortgage insurance, though they can carry a guarantee fee in its place. The standard version, the Guaranteed Rural Housing loan, or G-R-H, charges a one percent up-front guarantee that gets financed into the loan, plus a small annual fee of zero point three five percent, which is thirty-five basis points, spread across the monthly payments; it amortizes over thirty years with no prepayment penalty. Then there's the second flavor, the Homeownership Direct loan, or H-D, aimed at very-low-income borrowers, roughly fifty to eighty percent of the adjusted A-M-I. It can stretch thirty-three to thirty-eight years, may come with payment subsidies, and carries no guarantee fee at all.
va-and-usda.audio-va-and-usda-g10-p0: What really separates the four loan programs isn't the house or the borrower — it's who's on the hook for the lender's risk if the loan goes bad, and the exact word for it matters. A conventional loan gets bought and backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, with no government role at all. An F-H-A loan is insured by the federal government through HUD, so if the borrower defaults, the F-H-A repays the lender. A V-A loan is guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs, which covers part of the lender's loss. And a U-S-D-A loan is guaranteed by the Department of Agriculture, for rural borrowers. That single difference cascades into everything after it — the down payment, whether there's mortgage insurance, how income gets measured, and whether the loan can pass along to the next buyer.

fha.audio-fha-g0-p0: An F-H-A loan is insured by HUD, and that insurance is exactly what lets a borrower in with a smaller down payment and a lower credit score than a conventional loan would ever allow — as little as three and a half percent down, which puts you at a ninety-six and a half percent loan-to-value. The trade for that easy entry is mortgage insurance, and it shows up in two pieces. There's an up-front premium — M-I-P — set at one point seven five percent of the base loan, and most borrowers just roll it into the loan instead of paying it in cash at closing. Then there's an annual premium, collected a month at a time right inside the regular payment.
fha.audio-fha-g1-p0: How much you put down comes straight off your credit score, and F-H-A sorts borrowers into three tiers. A score of five hundred eighty or higher gets the floor — three and a half percent down, that ninety-six and a half percent loan-to-value. A score in the five hundred to five seventy-nine band still qualifies, but the down payment climbs to ten percent, a ninety percent loan-to-value. And below five hundred, there's no F-H-A financing at all. A weaker credit profile doesn't shut the door; it just asks for more cash up front, since the F-H-A's insurance only covers so much of the lender's risk.
fha.audio-fha-g2-p0: That annual M-I-P doesn't always run the full length of the loan — how long it sticks around turns on the down payment. With at least ten percent down, it falls off after eleven years. With anything less, you carry it for the life of the loan. And that's the spot most F-H-A borrowers land in: the majority come in with the minimum three and a half percent down, well under the ten-percent line, so the insurance rides along for the whole term. That permanent cost is why refinancing out of F-H-A becomes the goal once a borrower has built up enough equity.

construction-rehab.audio-construction-rehab-g0-p0: A lender isn't going to write a standard mortgage on a house that doesn't exist yet — there's no finished home standing there to secure the loan, no collateral to fall back on if the payments stop. Construction financing fills that gap. It funds the build in stages while the house goes up, then converts into an ordinary mortgage once the home is actually standing.
construction-rehab.audio-construction-rehab-g1-p0: At closing, the lender fronts the cost of the land plus an agreed slice of the build. Then, as each phase wraps up — foundation poured, framing finished — the builder asks for the next draw. The lender sends an inspector out to confirm the work before releasing that money, and the cycle just repeats: finish a phase, get it inspected, get the next draw, right up until the home is complete and fully funded. Through the whole build, the borrower is billed interest-only, and only on the money that's actually been drawn so far. So if two hundred thousand of a four-hundred-thousand-dollar build has been released, you're paying interest on that two hundred thousand and nothing more.
construction-rehab.audio-construction-rehab-g2-p0: A construction-to-permanent loan settles that finished build into an end loan — the permanent mortgage — and the borrower picks that end loan while construction is still going on. One-close handles the whole thing in a single settlement. Two-close closes the permanent loan separately, in its own second settlement. You can lock your rate for a long stretch to cover the build, but those locks get pricey once you push past ninety days, so timing the lock against how fast the house is actually going up really matters.
construction-rehab.audio-construction-rehab-g3-p0: When the house is already standing but needs real work, a rehab loan is the tool. It lends on the home's as-is value plus the cost of the planned renovations, releases the money against inspections as the work gets done, then converts to an end loan — the same rhythm as a construction loan. On the government side, you've got the F-H-A two-oh-three-K and the V-A Renovation loan. On the conventional side, there's Fannie Mae's HomeStyle and Freddie Mac's Renovation loan — and those two can stretch to cover second homes and investment properties, which the two-oh-three-K simply can't.

reverse-mortgages.audio-reverse-mortgages-g0-p0: A reverse mortgage flips the usual arrangement. Instead of paying the bank every month, an owner who's sixty-two or older pulls the equity out of the house as cash and keeps living right there — no monthly mortgage payment at all. The interest doesn't get paid down; it piles onto the balance and grows over time. And the loan only comes due when the last borrower finally leaves the home — sells it, moves out, or passes away. Picture a widow of seventy sitting on a paid-off house worth four hundred thousand; this lets her turn some of that into spending money without ever mailing in a payment.
reverse-mortgages.audio-reverse-mortgages-g1-p0: How much you can actually get comes down to the youngest borrower's age. Take a couple where one spouse is seventy and the other is sixty-three — the lender goes off sixty-three, the younger one, because that balance has more years to grow against the house. That age, along with the home's value and rates, sets the principal limit, which is the ceiling on what the loan will hand over. Older borrowers get a bigger number, since there's less time for interest to eat into the home's value. And however you decide to take the money, there's a leash in year one: you can't touch more than sixty percent of the principal limit up front.
reverse-mortgages.audio-reverse-mortgages-g1-p1: The money doesn't have to come all at once — you pick the shape it takes. Some folks grab a lump sum, the whole thing in one check. Others set up a line of credit and pull from it only when they need it, like a rainy-day account sitting against the house. And some want a steady monthly deposit, an annuity — and there you've got two flavors. Tenure keeps paying that same amount for as long as you're living in the home, while term hands you a bigger check but only for a set stretch of years, say ten, and then it stops.
reverse-mortgages.audio-reverse-mortgages-g2-p0: Nobody comes knocking for payment until something specific happens, and there are really four triggers. The last borrower dies and there's no surviving spouse still in the house. Or the home gets sold. Or the borrower's been out of the home — say, moved into assisted living — for more than twelve months straight. Or the property taxes and insurance lapse. And here's what makes the whole thing safe: the loan is non-recourse. So if that growing balance ever climbs past what the house is actually worth, the F-H-A insurance eats the difference — never the borrower, and never the kids who inherit.
reverse-mortgages.audio-reverse-mortgages-g3-p0: A few guardrails keep this loan from going sideways. Before anyone signs, every borrower has to sit through independent H-U-D-approved counseling — an outside expert walking them through the whole thing — and without that certificate in hand, the lender's lien isn't even enforceable. Then there's the LESA, the life expectancy set-aside: the lender can fence off a chunk of the proceeds up front and use it to pay the taxes and insurance itself, so those never lapse and never trip the loan. And if one spouse is under sixty-two — too young to be on the loan — they can still stay on the title as a non-borrowing spouse and live in that home for the rest of their life, as long as the borrowing spouse qualified in the first place.
reverse-mortgages.audio-reverse-mortgages-g4-p0: There are three flavors of these. The one you'll see most is the heck-um, the home equity conversion mortgage — it's F-H-A-insured and flexible about how the cash reaches you. Then a single-purpose reverse mortgage comes out of a state or local program and can only go toward one named thing, like a roof repair or the property tax bill — cheap, but narrow. And a proprietary one is a private, uninsured loan built for pricier homes that blow past the F-H-A ceiling. Now, because the customers here are elderly, the advertising gets watched closely: the MAP Rule — that's Regulation N — makes it a flat-out violation to fudge the costs, the payments, or a borrower's right to keep living in the home.

less-common-programs.audio-less-common-programs-g0-p0: Two fixed-rate programs break the level payment on purpose. On a graduated payment mortgage, the payments start out below the loan's true cost — that shortfall gets tacked onto the balance, so the loan actually grows for a while, which is negative amortization — and then the payments step up on a set schedule. A growth equity mortgage does the exact opposite: the payments run higher than required from day one, the extra goes straight to principal, and the loan gets paid off early. Say your required payment is fourteen hundred a month; a growth equity mortgage might have you paying sixteen hundred, with that extra two hundred knocking down principal every single month.
less-common-programs.audio-less-common-programs-g1-p0: Under a land contract, you move in and take possession, but you don't get the deed — you pay the seller directly, month after month, and title only passes to you once the full agreed sum is paid; walk away early and every payment you've made is forfeit. A package mortgage uses more than the property as collateral — it wraps in the land, the dwelling, and the personal property inside it, the furniture and the appliances, all appraised together as one bundle. And a reduction option mortgage is a fixed-rate loan that hands you a one-time chance to drop your rate without going through a full refinance, usually for a fee.

repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g0-p0: When you borrow money to buy a home, two separate things come back to the lender: the amount you borrowed, which is the principal, and the fee charged for borrowing it, which is the interest. You pay both of them down together, a little at a time, in one bill that lands on the same date every month.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g0-p1: A fixed-rate loan is the one most buyers picture, and the one most buyers end up signing. The rate is locked the day you close and it never budges, so your payment in year one is the exact same payment in year thirty, no matter what the wider economy does around you. Say rates jump two points next spring; yours doesn't move a dollar. That steadiness is why it's the default choice: you can build a household budget around a number that simply won't surprise you.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g0-p2: Everything else in this unit is a twist on that one arrangement — a change to the payment, a change to the payoff date, or both at once.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g1-p0: In the early years, your monthly payment barely dents what you borrowed, and there's a plain reason for it. Interest gets charged on whatever balance you still owe, and at the start that balance is as large as it will ever be, so most of each early payment goes toward the interest fee and only a sliver reaches the principal. As the balance shrinks, the interest slice shrinks right along with it, and more of every payment starts clearing what you actually borrowed. That slow tilt from interest toward principal is called amortization.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g1-p1: There's a turning point in that schedule called the crossover — the month where, inside a single payment, principal finally overtakes interest. On a thirty-year loan it doesn't land at the midpoint; it sits more than halfway through. And the interest really piles up: a two hundred thousand dollar loan at six percent pays two hundred thirty-one thousand, six hundred seventy-six dollars in interest across the full schedule — more than the amount you borrowed. Put even a little extra toward principal early and you pull that crossover forward and cut the total sharply, because a dollar of principal cleared today is a dollar you stop paying interest on for years to come.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g2-p0: An interest-only loan lets you pay just the interest fee for a set stretch at the beginning — often a few years — with nothing at all going toward the principal. The payment is smaller during that window, which sounds great, but the balance sits perfectly still: none of that money is buying you a share of the home.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g2-p1: It fits a fairly narrow kind of borrower — someone whose income arrives in big, irregular chunks, someone who fully expects to be earning a lot more before long, or an investor who plans to sell before the window ever closes. And there's a catch waiting on the far side. When the interest-only stretch ends, the loan re-casts, meaning the lender recalculates the payment to clear the entire balance over whatever years are left. Since nothing has been paid down, that fresh payment jumps hard.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g2-p2: Because a regular payment here isn't chipping away at the debt, an interest-only loan sits outside the safest category of home loan — the qualified mortgage, or Q-M, the federal standard for a loan the borrower can plainly afford. Interest-only counts as a non-Q-M feature, so the lender either keeps the loan on its own books or sells it off to a private investor instead of running it through the usual channels.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g3-p0: A balloon loan keeps your monthly payment low by setting it as if the loan stretched across a long thirty- or fifteen-year schedule — except it doesn't. After only a few years, the lender demands the whole remaining balance in a single lump, the balloon payment. When that day comes, you handle it one of three ways: sell the home, refinance into a brand-new loan, or pay the lump in full out of pocket.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g3-p1: Lenders label these with two numbers — the years until the lump comes due, then the long schedule the payment is based on. So a three twenty-seven is paid like a thirty-year loan but comes due at year three. That low payment is the trade for a genuine risk: a borrower who can't sell or refinance in time is suddenly owing the whole balance at once. It suits someone confident they'll move or refinance before the deadline, and it's a real hazard for someone who isn't.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g3-p2: Some balloon loans build in a safety valve called a conditional right to modify, or CRTM. It lets you convert to a fixed-rate loan instead of paying that lump, as long as you meet the loan's conditions and give written notice no later than forty-five days before the call.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g4-p0: Picture a borrower who comes into a chunk of money — a bonus, an inheritance — and puts it toward the loan. Normally the balance drops but the monthly payment holds steady, and the loan just finishes sooner. A re-cast flips that: the company that collects your payments — the servicer — recomputes a new, lower monthly payment against the reduced balance, spread across the same remaining years. The rate doesn't change and the payoff date doesn't move; only the monthly bill gets smaller.
repayment-structures.audio-repayment-structures-g4-p1: It's the right tool for someone who wants more breathing room in the monthly budget rather than an earlier payoff. The servicer decides whether to allow it in the first place, and it usually carries a fee.
